newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Irish punt revaluation seen hinging on economy, EMU.
newsitem.headline: Irish punt revaluation seen hinging on economy, EMU.

text.p: The difficult question of whether to revalue the Irish punt in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism may depend on longer-term developments in the Irish economy and its entry into EMU, EU officials and analysts say.

With the punt continuing to climb on the back of sterling's rapid ascent, there are some EU monetary officials who are wondering whether Ireland can afford to wait much longer before opting for a revaluation.

Until now, the widespread view among officials has been that such a step might be unwise, owing to the belief that the punt's rise would reverse itself once the long-awaited sell-off in sterling materialised.

But doubts over sterling's outlook -- there are those who question whether a near-term slide in the currency is likely -- and confidence in Ireland's structural economic change over the last few years have begun to turn the tide of opinion towards a possible revaluation.
"If you look at the progress of the Irish structural economy in the last few years it has strengthened and might need to be reflected in the exchange rate," said one EU official.
Evidence of sterling weakness emerged on Wednesday, but the currency still remains well above where many believe it should trade on a competitive basis.

EU officials say when put in a longer-term perspective, the punt may be undervalued against several leading European currencies, which together with Ireland's EMU aspirations, could argue for a modest revaluation of its central parity rate.

Some economists, however, said that while structural reform in Ireland may have provided it with lasting competitive benefits -- greater labour market flexibility is often cited as an example -- it is often difficult and perhaps somewhat risky to make such assessments.

"There may well be some structural medium-term reason for the punt to be higher, but on our estimates of fair value those sorts of arguments are difficult to support empirically," said Martin Brookes of Goldman Sachs in London.
Several analysts acknowleged that Ireland faced a tremendously difficult choice if sterling continued to remain strong, one that could be exacerbated if the dollar climbed further against the mark.
One rather important element of this complex picture are the implications for the French franc which currently commands the bottom spot in the ERM.

The type of scenario that EU monetary officials may want to avoid is where the punt breaches its 15 percent limit against the franc, say analysts. Under those circumstances French and Irish authorities would be obliged to intervene to correct the situation.
The added turbulence such a development would cause may be another reason why some are beginning to consider a revaluation of the punt as a good strategy.
The punt is currently trading about 11.5 percent above its central rate of 2.4111 against the Ecu and is about 12 percent above the French franc.
Ultimately, much will depend on what the Bundesbank thinks, and there are few analysts who believe Europe's most powerful central bank may be tilting toward the revaluation option.
Yet for Ireland, the big risk of such a decision would come if and when sterling declines and more importantly when the EU fixes the conversion rates for currencies entering EMU.
It is widely expected that the central parities within the ERM will used to lock currencies against one another in the runup to the euro's launch on January 1, 1999.
If Ireland revalues the punt and the EU decides to use the central parity option for locking rates, the Irish economy will have to live with a higher conversion rate.
Analysts say currency markets have already priced in a fairly large revaluation, with some estimates based on forward currency rates suggesting about a nine percent move.
